subject: history
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Who served as Elizabeth I's Secretary of State and most trusted advisor, later created Lord Burghley?
questions.explain: William Cecil (Lord Burghley) was Elizabeth's leading minister and chief advisor for most of her reign.

questions.q: Which of Elizabeth's ministers ran an extensive spy network to uncover Catholic plots against her?
questions.explain: Walsingham, Elizabeth's spymaster, built a network of informers that exposed plots such as the Babington Plot.

questions.q: The 1601 Poor Law recognised two categories of poor people. Which pair did it distinguish between?
options: The urban poor and the rural poor
The deserving (impotent) poor and the undeserving (idle) poor
The Catholic poor and the Protestant poor
The taxed poor and the untaxed poor
questions.explain: The deserving poor (old or sick) received relief, while the undeserving 'sturdy beggars' were punished for idleness.

questions.q: Why did Elizabeth encourage flattering portraits and the 'Gloriana' image of herself?
options: To raise money by selling the paintings abroad
To project majesty and legitimacy and strengthen loyalty to an unmarried queen
To disguise the fact that she was secretly Catholic
To encourage courtiers to become artists
questions.explain: Carefully controlled images were propaganda that presented Elizabeth as a powerful, semi-divine 'Virgin Queen'.

questions.q: Which combination of factors most contributed to rising poverty in Elizabethan England?
options: Population growth, inflation and poor harvests
A fall in the population and cheap food
questions.explain: A growing population, rising prices and bad harvests in the 1590s pushed many people into poverty and vagrancy.

questions.q: A vagrant with no work is arrested in an Elizabethan county. Which local official would be responsible for punishing him under the Poor Laws?
questions.explain: Justices of the Peace enforced law and order in the counties, including punishing vagabonds under the Poor Laws.

questions.q: Why did many Puritans oppose the new playhouses such as The Theatre and the Globe?
options: They believed theatres encouraged immorality and drew people away from church
They wanted the money spent on the navy instead
They thought plays were too expensive for the rich
questions.explain: Puritans saw playhouses as sources of sin and disorder that distracted people from godly worship.

questions.q: In 1570 the Pope issued a bull excommunicating Elizabeth and releasing Catholics from obedience to her. What was it called?
questions.explain: The papal bull Regnans in Excelsis (1570) excommunicated Elizabeth, sharpening fears of Catholic disloyalty.

questions.q: Which 1586 plot to assassinate Elizabeth and place Mary, Queen of Scots on the throne was uncovered by Walsingham?
questions.explain: The Babington Plot (1586) implicated Mary in coded letters and led directly to her trial and execution.

questions.q: In which year was Mary, Queen of Scots executed?
questions.explain: Mary was executed in 1587 after her involvement in the Babington Plot was proven.

questions.q: Why did the government regard Catholic seminary priests and Jesuits arriving from abroad as a serious threat?
options: They refused to pay any taxes to the Crown
They aimed to keep Catholicism alive and could encourage rebellion against the Protestant queen
They wanted to take control of the English navy
They were spies sent to steal exploration maps
questions.explain: Missionary priests such as Edmund Campion were seen as agents of the Pope and Spain who threatened Elizabeth's Protestant state.

questions.q: A wealthy landowner repeatedly refuses to attend Church of England services and pays fines for doing so. What term describes him?
questions.explain: Recusants were Catholics who refused to attend Anglican services and were fined for their absence.

questions.q: In which year did Philip II of Spain launch the Armada against England?
questions.explain: The Spanish Armada was launched in 1588 and was defeated by English forces and bad weather.

questions.q: Which factor contributed most directly to the defeat of the Spanish Armada at the Battle of Gravelines?
options: English fireships scattered the Spanish fleet, breaking its crescent formation
The Spanish ran out of gunpowder before the battle began
The English navy heavily outnumbered the Spanish
The Spanish commander surrendered without a fight
questions.explain: Fireships sent into Calais harbour broke the Armada's formation, exposing it to English attack at Gravelines.

questions.q: After the Armada's defeat, storms drove Spanish ships around Scotland and Ireland. How did Elizabethan propaganda interpret this?
options: As bad luck that damaged England's reputation
As proof that Spain would soon invade again
As a sign of God's favour towards Protestant England — the 'Protestant Wind'
As evidence that the English navy had failed
questions.explain: Propaganda presented the storms as the 'Protestant Wind', showing that God supported Elizabeth's Protestant realm.

questions.q: Which ship did Sir Francis Drake command on his circumnavigation of the globe?
questions.explain: Drake circumnavigated the world aboard the Golden Hind (originally named the Pelican), returning in 1580.

questions.q: Why was Drake's completion of a circumnavigation in 1580 significant for England?
options: It brought great wealth from plundered Spanish treasure and boosted national prestige
It ended all conflict with Spain
It established a permanent colony in the New World
It opened a trade route to Russia for the first time
questions.explain: Drake returned laden with Spanish treasure, enriching Elizabeth and raising England's standing; he was knighted in 1581.

questions.q: Sir Walter Raleigh sponsored attempts to establish an English colony in the New World. What was the settlement called?
questions.explain: Raleigh's colony at Roanoke in Virginia failed and its settlers vanished, becoming known as the 'Lost Colony'.

questions.q: Which of the following was a key reason English sailors undertook long voyages of exploration in this period?
options: The desire for trade, wealth and new markets
A ban on farming in England
Orders from the Pope to spread Catholicism
A shortage of ships in Spain
questions.explain: Explorers sought new trade routes, precious goods and markets, alongside adventure and rivalry with Spain.

questions.q: An Elizabethan navigator needs to work out his latitude during a long ocean voyage. Which instrument would help him do this?
questions.explain: Navigators used the astrolabe to measure the height of the sun or stars and estimate their latitude at sea.
